title: Lab – Medical history in ophthalmology
html:
Source: Medical history in ophthalmology.pptx – 33 slides

Medical history in Ophthalmology #1

Medical history #2

  • May suggest the disorder/ cause of ocular symptoms
  • May identify parts of clinical exam that require special consideration
  • May suggest the importance of additional investigations
  • May suggest a systemic disorder
  • May identify risk factors for possible future disorders

Potential ocular complaints #3

  • Ocular congestion
  • Progressive loss of vision
  • Acute loss of vision
  • Diplopia
  • Strabismus
  • “Spots” in front of the eyes
  • Ocular discomfort
  • Proptosis
  • Trauma

1. Ocular congestion #4

  • Medical history:
  • - recurrent → keratitis/ iridocyclitis
  • - hyperopia → acute angle-closure glaucoma
  • - contact lens wear → corneal erosion/ ulceration

1. Ocular congestion #5

  • Symptoms:
  • - itching → allergic conjunctivitis
  • - stinging → infectious conjunctivitis
  • - pain → indicates a more severe disorder
  • - photophobia, intense pain when reading → iridocyclitis

1. Ocular congestion #6

  • Ocular discharge:
  • - watery → viral conjunctivitis, corneal erosion
  • - purulent → bacterial conjunctivitis
  • - mucous → allergic conjunctivitis

1. Ocular congestion #7

  • Uni/ bilateral:
  • - bilateral → infectious conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis
  • - unilateral → iridocyclitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma

1. Ocular congestion #8

  • Vision:
  • - mildly decreased occasionally → conjunctivitis
  • - significant visual loss → severe disorder

1. Ocular congestion #9

  • Associated systemic disorders:
  • - upper respiratory tract infections → infectious conjunctivitis
  • - history of allergy → allergic conjunctivitis
  • - sarcoidosis, ankylosing spondylitis → iridocyclitis
  • - conjunctive tissue disorders → scleritis
  • - rosacea → blepharitis/ conjunctivitis

2. Progressive visual loss #10

  • Medical history:
  • - diabetes mellitus/ systemic steroid treatment/ hypocalcemia → cataracts
  • - diabetes mellitus → diabetic retinopathy
  • - chloroquine → toxic retinopathy

2. Progressive visual loss #11

  • Ocular history:
  • - ocular contusion/ malignant myopia/ recurrent uveitis/ topical steroids/ exposure to UV light/ infrared irradiation → cataracts
  • - topical steroids → cataracts/ glaucoma

2. Progressive visual loss #12

  • Family history:
  • - glaucoma
  • - hereditary disorders of cornea/ retina/ optic nerve

2. Progressive visual loss #13

  • Vision:
  • - worse at near → macular disorders/ posterior subcapsular cataracts
  • - worse at distance → nuclear cataracts

3. Acute visual loss #14

  • Onset:
  • - hyperacute → retinal artery occlusion
  • - suddenly noticed → retinal vein occlusion/ macular hemorrhage
  • - recurrent transient visual loss → emboli/ ischemic optic neuropathy/ intracranial hypertension

3. Acute visual loss #15

  • Vision:
  • - significant visual loss → retinal artery occlusion
  • - “fogging” → majority of disorders
  • - distorted image → macular disorders

3. Acute visual loss #16

  • Affected visual field area:
  • - only central → macular disorders
  • - right or left → hemianopia
  • - progressive from periphery toward the center → retinal detachment/ retinal arterial embolus/ migraine

3. Acute visual loss #17

  • Associated ocular symptoms:
  • - pain, red eye → acute glaucoma
  • - pain with eye movement → optic neuritis/ posterior scleritis

4. Diplopia #18

  • Binocular/ monocular:
  • - binocular → paralytic strabismus
  • - monocular → nuclear cataracts/ lens subluxation

4. Diplopia #19

  • Display of the two images:
  • - next to the other → VIth nerve palsy
  • - vertical/ oblique → any other cause of paralytical strabismus

4. Diplopia #20

  • Intermittent:
  • - decompensated latent strabismus
  • - myasthenia gravis
  • - orbital thyroid disease

4. Diplopia #21

  • History of trauma:
  • - VIth nerve palsy
  • - orbital fracture

4. Diplopia #22

  • Medical history:
  • - vascular risk factors
  • - thyroid disease
  • - intracranial hypertension
  • - myasthenia gravis

5. Childhood strabismus #23

  • Medical history:
  • - perinatal risk factors: mother’s infections/ substance abuse/ prematurity/ prolonged labor/ growth delay/ neurologic disorders
  • - current health: recent systemic viral disease/ neurologic disorders

5. Childhood strabismus #24

  • Family history:
  • - strabismus
  • - refractive errors - hyperopia
  • - amblyopia

5. Childhood strabismus #25

  • Ocular history:
  • - refractive errors
  • - treatment of strabismus/ amblyopia
  • - congenital cataract

6. “Spots” in front of the eyes #26

  • Myodesopsia = floaters:
  • - myopia/ elders → due to vitreous degeneration
  • - sudden onset → posterior vitreous detachment (risk of retinal detachment)
  • - sudden onset and decreased vision → vitreous hemorrhage
  • - inflammatory cells in the vitreous → posterior uveitis

6. “Spots” in front of the eyes #27

  • Phosphenes:
  • - transient/ related to head or eye movement → acute posterior vitreous detachment
  • - recurrent, duration of few minutes, zigzag → migraine

7. Proptosis #28

  • - differential diagnosis with pseudo-proptosis: malignant myopia/ contralateral enophthalmos (trauma)
  • - most common cause of proptosis → thyroid disease
  • - loss of vision → urgent referral to ophthalmology

8. Eye discomfort #29

  • Medical history:
  • - conjunctive tissue disease/ thyroid disease → dry eye
  • allergy → allergic conjunctivitis
  • rosacea → kerato-conjunctivitis

8. Eye discomfort #30

  • Ocular history:
  • - contact lens wear → allergy/ intolerance
  • topical medication → allergy

8. Eye discomfort #31

  • Presentation:
  • - worse in warm and dry rooms/ worse at the end of the day/ women at menopause → dry eye
  • dry crust on eyelid’s margin/ worse in the morning → blepharitis

9. Trauma #32

  • Medical history:
  • mechanism of trauma: possible intraocular foreign body?
  • type of injury: sharp object (wound)/ non-sharp object (contusion)/ chemical injury (burns)
  • systemic comorbidities
  • in case general anesthesia is required: time of last meal, medications, allergies

9. Trauma #33

  • Pain → does not correlate with severity
  • Loss of vision → does not correlate with severity
